Hydrogen bonding wins. Same family? Size wins."); chem-m7-c08b (polar C=O, dipole–dipole forces); chem-m7-c03 (dispersion forces depend on the number of electrons; the water lattice); chem-m7-c01 (naming rules, locants); chem-m6-c01 (a Brønsted-Lowry base takes a proton; NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻; H₃O⁺); chem-m6-c02 (acid + base → salt); chem-m6-c05 (weak means partly ionised; weak is not dilute). Not assumed: amine, amide, primary, secondary and tertiary amines, "-amine" and "-amide" naming, N- prefixes, alkylammonium salts, why an amide is not basic.
progression.startsWith: Identify the nitrogen functional groups. The video opens: Leave seafood out too long, and it smells fishy. Much of that smell comes from trimethylamine, an amine. Squeeze some lemon juice over it, and the smell fades.
progression.stopsAfter: identifying, classifying and naming amines and amides up to C8 with methyl or ethyl groups; explaining their boiling points and solubility against alcohols, carboxylic acids and alkanes, and within each series; writing the equation for an amine in water and with hydrochloric acid; explaining why an amine is a weak base and an amide is close to neutral; comparing a carboxylic acid with an amine by proton behaviour, litmus, the hydrogen carbonate test and the salt they form. No Kb, no aromatic amines, no polyamides.

teaching.task: Amines and amides both contain nitrogen. An amine's solution turns red litmus blue and its smell vanishes with lemon juice, but an amide leaves litmus unchanged. What does the C=O beside an amide's nitrogen change, and how does an organic base differ from an organic acid?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the fishy smell is an amine; lemon juice removes it; amines turn red litmus blue, but ethanamide, also a nitrogen compound, does not (1); (2) an amine is ammonia with carbon groups replacing hydrogens; the nitrogen keeps a lone pair; classify by counting carbon groups on N, not the alcohol rule (2); (3) naming amines: "-amine", N- for groups on the nitrogen (3); (4) an amide is a C=O bonded straight to N, like an ester with N in place of the single-bonded O, made by condensation when an acid and an amine are heated strongly; naming "-amide", C1 at the C=O (4); (5) N is less electronegative than O, so N–H is less polar and amine hydrogen bonds are weaker: amines boil below alcohols (5); (6) among isomers, fewer N–H hydrogens means fewer hydrogen bonds (two, one, none), so boiling points fall; tertiary amines cannot hydrogen bond to each other; small amines mix with water (6); (7) primary amides have two N–H hydrogens and a C=O that takes hydrogen bonds, so each molecule makes more hydrogen bonds and they build networks, boiling far above acids, which pair off as dimers; longer chains raise boiling points in every series (screen row) (7); (8) in water, the amine's lone pair takes a proton, leaving OH⁻; the raised OH⁻ concentration turns red litmus blue; reversible, lies left: a weak base (8); (9) with a stronger acid the proton transfer goes to completion: an ionic salt that barely evaporates, so the smell goes (9); (10) in an amide the C=O beside the N draws in and shares the lone pair; sharing loosens the grip on a proton (as in c09's carboxylate), so it barely takes a proton; no O–H, so not an acid either: litmus unchanged (10); (11) organic acid against organic base: gives a proton from O–H, takes a proton with a lone pair; litmus by the raised H₃O⁺ or OH⁻ concentration, and the hydrogen carbonate test (screen chip); together they make a salt at room temperature, and only strong heating makes an amide (11); memory aid (12); two attempts and brief feedback (13 to 16); handoff (17); key notes (18).
teaching.conversationalApproach: seafood left out smells fishy because of an amine, lemon juice removes the smell, and an amine's solution turns red litmus blue while an amide leaves litmus unchanged, so the video asks what the C=O beside an amide's nitrogen changes and how an organic base differs from an organic acid. An amine is ammonia with carbon chains replacing hydrogens, and the nitrogen keeps its lone pair; amines are classified by counting the carbon groups on the nitrogen and named with amine. An amide has a C=O bonded straight to the nitrogen, like an ester with nitrogen in place of the single-bonded oxygen, and is named with amide. A primary amine hydrogen bonds like an alcohol but more weakly, because nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, and among isomers fewer N-H hydrogens means a lower boiling point; amides form a network of hydrogen bonds and boil higher than acids of similar size. In water the amine's lone pair takes a proton, raising the hydroxide concentration, so it is a weak base, and with hydrochloric acid it forms an ionic salt; an amide is barely a base because the C=O pulls the lone pair in and shares it. A carboxylic acid gives a proton and an amine takes one. The memory aid is amines are organic ammonia, a free pair makes a base. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Leave seafood out too long, and it smells fishy. Much of that smell comes from trimethylamine, an amine. Squeeze some lemon juice over it, and the smell fades. The amine's solution turns red litmus blue, so it's a base. Ethanamide has a nitrogen too, but its solution leaves litmus unchanged. So why is one nitrogen compound a base, while the other barely is?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "The three amines below all have the molecular formula C₄H₁₁N. A: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂, boiling point 78 °C. B: CH₃CH₂NHCH₂CH₃, boiling point 55 °C. C: CH₃CH₂N(CH₃)₂, boiling point 37 °C. (a) Give the IUPAC name of amine A, and classify amines B and C as primary, secondary or tertiary. (b) Explain the order of the boiling points, with reference to the intermolecular forces present." New molecules (scenes use C2 and C3 amines; the site uses the C2 pair); same formula, so dispersion is similar and the number of N–H hydrogens (2, 1, 0) decides, the rule scene 6 teaches on the C3 isomers (Revision 2, learning L1), here transferred to new C4 molecules and values; tests naming, classification by carbon groups on N, and the cause. Crossed mistake: "All three amines hydrogen bond to each other." (the tertiary amine has no N–H to give; L16 card 2 and Q6 pattern). (A2) "Separate aqueous solutions of propanoic acid, propan-1-amine and propanamide are prepared. (a) Predict the effect of each solution on red litmus paper and on blue litmus paper. (b) Explain the results for propan-1-amine and for propanamide." New set (scenes use ethanoic acid, ethanamine and ethanamide); tests the acid against base comparison and the shared lone pair. Crossed mistake: "Propanamide turns blue litmus red, because it has a C=O group like a carboxylic acid." (L16 card 4 Common Error).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "investigate the nomenclature of organic chemicals, up to C8, using IUPAC conventions, including simple methyl and ethyl branched chains, including: (ACSCH127); alkanes; alkenes; alkynes; alcohols (primary, secondary and tertiary); aldehydes and ketones; carboxylic acids; amines and amides; halogenated organic compounds" This video covers amines and amides only (hydrocarbons chem-m7-c01 and g01; haloalkanes chem-m7-c04a; alcohols chem-m7-c05; aldehydes and ketones chem-m7-c08b; carboxylic acids chem-m7-c09; esters chem-m7-c10). "investigate the structural formulae, properties and functional group including:; primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols; aldehydes and ketones (ACSCH127); amines and amides; carboxylic acids" This video covers amines and amides (alcohols chem-m7-c05; aldehydes and ketones chem-m7-c08b; carboxylic acids chem-m7-c09). "explain the properties within and between the homologous series of carboxylic acids amines and amides with reference to the intermolecular and intramolecular bonding present" This video covers amines and amides, within their series and against alcohols, carboxylic acids and alkanes; carboxylic acids were chem-m7-c09. "investigate the differences between an organic acid and organic base" This video covers the organic base (amines), the amide as a nitrogen compound that is barely basic, and the comparison of a carboxylic acid with an amine (route review change 3). The acid half was chem-m7-c09. this video starts by identifying the amine and amide functional groups, and stops at comparing amines, amides and carboxylic acids for basicity, intermolecular forces and reactions. It teaches: an amine is ammonia with one or more hydrogens replaced by carbon groups, and its nitrogen keeps a lone pair (a pair of electrons not used in bonding); classification by the number of carbon groups bonded to the nitrogen (primary 1, secondary 2, tertiary 3), not the alcohol rule (propan-2-amine is a primary amine); naming primary amines ("alkan-x-amine": ethanamine, propan-1-amine, propan-2-amine) and secondary and tertiary amines with N- prefixes (N-methylethanamine, N,N-dimethylethanamine); an amide is a C=O bonded straight to a nitrogen (–CONH₂), like an ester with the single-bonded oxygen replaced by nitrogen, formed by condensation of a carboxylic acid with an amine (or ammonia) when heated strongly, losing water; naming amides ("alkanamide", the C=O carbon is C1 and counted in the chain: ethanamide, propanamide, N-methylethanamide); intramolecular bonds are polar covalent (N–H, C–N, C=O); hydrogen bonding in primary and secondary amines is weaker than in alcohols because N is less electronegative than O, so the N–H bond is less polar (propan-1-amine 48 °C against propan-1-ol 97 °C, same electron count); among isomers, fewer N–H hydrogens means fewer hydrogen bonds and a lower boiling point (propan-1-amine, two N–H, 48 °C; N-methylethanamine, one, about 37 °C); tertiary amines have no N–H, so they cannot hydrogen bond to each other (trimethylamine 3 °C); small amines mix with water because water hydrogen bonds to the lone pair; primary amides have two N–H hydrogens and a C=O that takes hydrogen bonds, so each molecule makes more hydrogen bonds, building networks, and they boil much higher than acids of the same electron count, which mostly pair off as dimers (propanamide 213 °C against propanoic acid 141 °C); within each series, longer chains add dispersion, so boiling points rise; an amine's lone pair takes a proton from water (RNH₂ + H₂O ⇌ RNH₃⁺ + OH⁻), so its solution turns red litmus blue, but the equilibrium lies to the left (a weak base; Module 6 recall: ammonia); with hydrochloric acid it forms an ionic alkylammonium salt (ethylammonium chloride), which barely evaporates, so the fishy smell fades (the lemon trick); in an amide the C=O beside the nitrogen draws the lone pair in and shares it across N, C and O (the same C=O effect as the carboxylate in c09: sharing loosens the grip on a proton, which made the acid stronger and makes the amide barely a base), so it takes almost no protons from water and its solution is close to neutral; it is not acidic either (no O–H; its N–H hydrogens barely let go); the comparison: a carboxylic acid gives a proton from its O–H, an amine takes one with its lone pair; both are weak; the acid raises the hydronium ion concentration and turns blue litmus red (and fizzes with sodium hydrogen carbonate, a c09 recall on screen), the amine raises the hydroxide ion concentration and turns red litmus blue; mixed at room temperature they form a salt by proton transfer (methylammonium ethanoate), with no water formed; strong heating is needed to drive off water and make an amide. Not here: Kb and pKb values or calculations (not in the 2017 dotpoints; author note d); aniline and aryl amines (aromatic, beyond the course; the site marks phenol as extension, and aniline is the same case); amide resonance structures with formal charges (author note e); restricted rotation and peptide planarity (Biology and chem-m7-c15 territory); amide hydrolysis (author note f; root decision in Revision 2: no dotpoint needs it); polyamides and nylon (chem-m7-c15); quaternary ammonium detergents (chem-m7-c12 mentions cationic detergents); diamines putrescine and cadaverine (site hook; author note g); reaction of amines with sodium metal.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c09, plus nitrogen: carbon skeleton ink; hydrogens soft grey; main chain pale blue; branches and carbon groups on N amber; oxygen brick red; nitrogen indigo with the letter N printed; the lone pair as two small indigo dots; the amine group ringed indigo; the amide group ringed as one shape, red at the C=O and indigo at the N; δ− and δ+ small in navy; hydrogen bonds dotted violet; dipole–dipole dotted teal; dispersion dotted pale blue; the transferring proton in the chem-m6-c01 proton colour; OH⁻ in the Module 6 anion colour; the shared lone pair as c09's grey-violet glow. Board layout (constant): top-left the short task chip ("Base or not?", "Classify", "Name it", "Forces", "Proton test", "Acid or base?"); centre the structure board, one molecule or one pair at a time; the boiling point strip at the right only in scenes 5 to 7; plates small or medium at the left or right only in scenes 1, 2, 8, 9, 10, 11, 16 and 17. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends; the previous case leaves before the next one draws. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 27 Oct by contact sheet): `m6-lemon-v1.png` (a whole lemon and a cut half with two leaves; scenes 1 and 9, small); `m6-litmus-red-v1.png` and `m6-litmus-blue-v1.png` (aligned pair; scenes 1, 8, 10, 11 and 16); `m5x-ammonia-bottle-v1.png` (amber reagent bottle with a blank label; scene 2, small, labelled "ammonia solution, NH₃(aq)", as chem-m6-c01 did); chem-m7-c09's `m7-litmus-blue-strip-v1.png` (commissioned there; scenes 10, 11 and 16); `m6-soap-bar-v1.png` (handoff, small). Not used: `m6-hcl-ammonia-gas-reaction-v1.png` (the gas-phase ring is Module 6's evidence; not needed here); `m7-polymer-objects-v1.png` (nylon belongs to c15). One new plate (Assets).
